To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

cortically induced c-fos expression in different auditory thalamo-cortical nuclei after bilateral cochlear removal is differentially dependent on corticofugal input and that the temporal pattern of this expression correlates with the temporal pattern of corticofugal activity in different thalamo-corticofugal nuclei.
cortically induced c-fos expression in the thalamus and inferior colliculus after bilateral cochlear removal is time and subnucleus dependent.
corticofugal stimulation can induce c-fos in MGB neurons and that this effect varies in time after cochlear ablations.
In summary, our research is concerned with

the role of the auditory corticofugal pathway in regulating the activity of neurons in the MGB and IC, and the time course of the cortically activated FOS expression in these nuclei after unilateral and bilateral cochlear ablations.
the time course of cortically evoked Fos expression in thalamic nuclei and midbrain after unilateral cochlear ablation.
the effects of bilateral cochlear ablations on Fos expression in auditory thalamic and midbrain nuclei after bicuculline administration in the auditory cortex.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
corticofugal projections are crucial in eliciting cortically induced Fos expression in auditory thalamic and midbrain nuclei.

corticofugal projections from the cortex to the MGB and IC, although important in normal auditory processing, are not essential for auditory processing after bilateral cochlear damage, at least not for the first 30 days after the damage.
corticofugal inputs to the MGB and the IC, which are normally modulated by ascending auditory inputs, are not completely eliminated by cochlear ablation in adult rats.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

cortically evoked Fos expression is differentially regulated in the auditory thalamus, and the temporal profile of Fos expression in IC neurons after bilateral cochlear lesion is similar to that of MGB neurons.

corticofugal inputs are important for the expression of Fos after cochlear ablations, and that corticofugally driven Fos expression in auditory thalamic and midbrain nuclei is time dependent and may be associated with the denervation sensitivity of the neurons.

cortically induced Fos expressions in different MGB and IC subnucleus after bilateral cochlear denervation are highly dependent on corticofugal activity, which is in turn regulated by the state of denervation hypersensitivity of the MGB and IC neurons.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the corticofugal system plays a major role in regulating the Fos expression in MGB neurons after cochlear ablations.
the corticofugal system can play a significant role in modulating the neuronal activity of auditory thalamic nuclei after bilateral cochlear deafferentation.
cortically induced Fos expression in MGB neurons after cochlear ablations is a time- and subnucleus-specific phenomenon.
